tour.title: Genesis 6:1-4: Watchers, Giants, and the Flood
tour.intro: This tour first locates Genesis 6:1-4 in the spreading violence of Genesis 4–6, then lets you hear the main readings of the “sons of God” and the Nephilim without pretending the debate is settled. It ends by showing why this strange paragraph functions as the immediate prelude to the flood.

steps.why: Begin with the passage’s narrative purpose rather than its most sensational details. The teachers ask, “Why is this here?” and answer that the rebellion and brokenness are getting worse: humanity is supposed to spread God’s image, but “the exact opposite is happening.” They describe the result as a cosmic rebellion “spiraling out of control,” which prepares you to hear the flood as judgment on creation’s unraveling.

Now hear the strongest spiritual-beings reading. The teachers say “the phrase appears about half a dozen times in the Hebrew Bible, and it always has the same meaning,” referring to beings in God’s heavenly court. They connect “saw ... good” and “took” to Genesis 3, calling this “a fall narrative,” and describe the Nephilim as “mighty warriors” and “men of the name” within an ancient story-world of divine-human warrior kings.
steps.episodeTitle: God’s Spirit in the Flood Narrative

steps.why: Use this clip to slow down and separate what Genesis says from later interpretation. The teacher lays out three major views—“spiritual beings,” “human rulers,” and people from the godly line—and stresses that the passage’s main role is to portray the “decay and depravity of the human race.” Most importantly for the Nephilim question, the teacher says they are called “mighty men of old” and “men of renown,” but Genesis does not clearly say they were the offspring of the union.

End by hearing a sustained alternative to the angelic interpretation. This teacher says the “sons of God” are believers—the “true church”—who rebel by marrying into the “Church of Cain” or false church. On this reading, the 120 years is not a new maximum lifespan but the interval before the flood, “a time for repentance,” giving the passage a direct role as a warning and a final window of mercy before judgment.
steps.episodeTitle: 40 Minutes In The Old Testament: Episode 11

tour.closing: You have now heard both the major identifications and the larger biblical logic: Genesis 6:1-4 is deliberately strange, but it is not an isolated monster story. Whether you favor the heavenly-beings reading, the human-rulers reading, or the godly-line reading, the paragraph functions as an escalation of rebellion and violence immediately before the flood.

caveats: Clips on ad-inserted hosts (Megaphone: ask-nt-wright, spoken-gospel) can land up to ~2 minutes off against today’s stream. This is a known corpus-wide drift, not a bug in this tour.
A tour is model output over machine transcripts. The "why" text should report what a transcript says; it is not a claim that the speaker is right.

The player streams each episode straight from its publisher. A few hosts (Substack’s CDN, for one) refuse hotlinked requests and the step will say so and offer the URL instead — the clip boundaries are still good, the playback path is not.
